## Why odin?

A compartmental model is a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

- R's standard solver, `deSolve`, integrates these with compiled Fortran
  routines — the solver itself is fast
- The slow part is the model function: you write it in R, and the solver
  calls back into R at every integration step
- You can write the model function in C (deSolve supports this), but doing
  it by hand is tedious and easy to get wrong

odin does this translation for you:

- You write the equations in a language that looks like R
- odin translates them to C, compiles them, and links them to deSolve's
  solver
- The model runs at compiled speed — this matters when you fit models or
  run many scenarios
- odin also handles the bookkeeping: state vectors, initial conditions,
  array indexing

## The declarative idea

odin code is declarative. It is not executed as R code; it is parsed and
compiled. You write what the equations are, not how to compute them, so
the order of the lines does not matter.

## The SIR model

The classic SIR model splits a population of $N$ people into Susceptible,
Infectious and Recovered:

$$
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta SI, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta SI - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I
$$

- $\beta$ — transmission rate
- $\gamma$ — recovery rate; $1/\gamma$ is the mean infectious period
- The basic reproduction number is $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$

This is the density-dependent formulation: transmission is proportional to
the number of infectious people, so $R_0$ scales with the population size
$N$ — and $\beta$ therefore depends on the population you are modelling.

## Anatomy of an odin model {.scrollable}

An odin model has three ingredients: derivatives (`deriv()`), initial
conditions (`initial()`) and parameters. In this first version we fix the
parameter values directly in the code:

```{r}
#| message: true
library(odin)

# verbose = TRUE so we can watch odin generate and compile the C code
sir_generator <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- 1000  # total population size
  I0    <- 1     # initial number infectious
  beta  <- 2e-4  # transmission rate (R0 = beta * N / gamma = 2)
  gamma <- 0.1   # recovery rate (10-day infectious period)
}, verbose = TRUE)
```

## What just happened?

The messages show odin generating C code from the equations and compiling
it. From this point on, running the model involves no R code at all.

The compiler warnings you may see (`unused variable`, `format specifies...`)
come from the C template inside the odin package — odin regenerates it on
every compile, so there is nothing in your model to correct. They sit in
code paths this model never hits; the place to fix them is upstream in odin.

Note two things:

- `odin::odin({...})` parsed and compiled the equations. If that line runs
  without error, the model is ready to use.
- The result, `sir_generator`, is not a model — it is a model generator: a
  factory that creates model instances.

## Running the model

Create an instance and run it over a vector of times:

```{r}
sir <- sir_generator$new()

t <- seq(0, 150, by = 1)
y <- sir$run(t)

head(y)
```

`y` is a data frame with one column per compartment plus time `t`, one row
per requested time point.

## Plotting with base R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
matplot(y[, "t"], y[, c("S", "I", "R")],
        type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        col = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "darkgreen"),
        xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Number of people")
legend("right", legend = c("S", "I", "R"), lwd = 2,
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "darkgreen"), bty = "n")
```

Here $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma = 2$.

## Making parameters changeable: `user()` {.scrollable}

This model works, but the parameters are fixed in the compiled C code. To
try a different `beta` you would have to edit the model definition and
recompile, which gets awkward when you want to compare several scenarios.

`user()` solves this. Declaring a parameter with `user(default)` makes it
settable when the model instance is created, with the default used when
you don't set it. Only the parameter block changes:

```{r}
sir_generator <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)  # can now be changed at $new() time
  I0    <- user(1)
  beta  <- user(2e-4)
  gamma <- user(0.1)
})
```

- `sir_generator$new()` uses all the defaults.
- `sir_generator$new(beta = 3e-4)` overrides just `beta`, without
  recompiling — the compiled C code is reused.
- `m$contents()` shows the parameter values an instance is using.

## One generator, many scenarios

Scenarios are now cheap — pass new parameter values to `$new()`:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
beta_values <- c(3e-4, 2e-4, 1.5e-4)
plot(NULL, xlim = range(t), ylim = c(0, 350),
     xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Infectious (I)")
for (b in beta_values) {
  m <- sir_generator$new(beta = b)
  lines(t, m$run(t)[, "I"], lwd = 2,
        col = hcl.colors(length(beta_values), "Berlin")[which(beta_values == b)])
}
legend("topright", legend = paste("beta =", beta_values,
                                  "(R0 =", beta_values * 1000 / 0.1, ")"),
       col = hcl.colors(length(beta_values), "Berlin"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

Compilation happens once; every scenario after that is just `$new()` and
`$run()`.

## Notes on scenarios

- Only the parameters you name are changed; the rest keep their defaults
- No recompilation needed — the C code is compiled once, at generator
  creation

## Tracking extra quantities: cumulative incidence

Sometimes you want a quantity that is not a compartment — for example the
total number of infections so far. Add another derivative that accumulates
it:

```{r}
sir_inc <- odin::odin({
  deriv(S) <- -beta * S * I
  deriv(I) <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
  deriv(R) <- gamma * I
  deriv(cum_inc) <- beta * S * I   # accumulates new infections
  initial(S) <- N0 - I0
  initial(I) <- I0
  initial(R) <- 0
  initial(cum_inc) <- 0
  N0    <- user(1000)
  I0    <- user(1)
  beta  <- user(2e-4)
  gamma <- user(0.1)
})
```

## The final size of the epidemic

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
y <- sir_inc$new()$run(t)
plot(y[, "t"], y[, "cum_inc"], type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Cumulative infections")
```

The final value of `cum_inc` is the final size of the epidemic: about 80%
of the population. The epidemic dies out before everyone is infected
because once prevalence is high, each infectious person infects fewer than
one susceptible on average.

## Exercise 1

**Exercise 1.1 — What does $R_0$ control?**
Using `sir_generator`, run the model with `beta` chosen so that $R_0$ is
1.2, 1.5 and 2.5 (keep `gamma = 0.1`; remember $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$).
Plot the three `I` curves on one plot. What happens to the peak height and
peak timing as $R_0$ increases?

**Exercise 1.2 — Threshold behaviour**
Set `beta = 8e-5` (so $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma = 0.8 < 1$) and run the
model. What happens, and why does no epidemic occur?

## Recap

- odin models are equations, not code: `deriv()`, `initial()`, parameters
- `odin::odin({...})` compiles the equations to C and returns a generator
- `generator$new()` creates an instance; `$run(t)` integrates it
- `user(default)` makes a parameter settable at `$new()` — one
  compilation, unlimited scenarios
- Add a `deriv()` line for derived quantities like cumulative incidence
